Funny story about this stuff: I work in the toll collection business. We like to use plate-reader algorithms with violation enforcement cameras and on roads that collect "tolls by plate", since it's way cheaper than hiring people to read every plate image. Back in 2009, I was in a boardroom at one agency, and a bunch of camera vendors were giving a demo of their stuff. Most of them were specific to the toll industry and it was the standard IR camera with an ALPR backend that you feed it a plate and it spits out a result and confidence level.

But then this one vendor had showed up, who mostly made cameras for police cars. And they demoed a system with a Google Maps type interface where you could query it and see every "hit" on a particular plate, and zoom in and out geographically and increase/decrease the time scale. And the guy was just blabbing and showing how great it was, "look here, we can see the guy goes to a liquor store typically on Wednesday nights". And the room got super quiet, because everyone realized that this was absolutely not something we wanted our industry to be associated with.

And that was in 2009, and now it's all over the place. Welcome to the future!

Do any of those gimmicky plate blockers actually work?

Not the spray ones. When those started getting press, one of my clients asked about them so I did some testing. I bought a couple different sprays marketed as being able to defeat red-light and speed cameras, plus tried rolling my own with various types of retroreflective lacquer. (The general idea is that most plates have a retroreflective background, but the plate digits are not reflective. Those sprays claim that by covering the digits in retroreflective lacquer, they cause the flash to blind the camera. In real life that only works with normal color cameras using a visible light flash mounted very close to the lens, like a consumer camera or a phone, and then only if you shoot the plate from a close distance).

When I tested agaisnt several toll system camera / illuminator combinations, the best result I got was a slight graying of the characters. Police car cameras don't use a flash anyway, they use a continuous IR illuminator so those sprays couldn't work on them even if they managed to work against toll / red light / speed cameras.

They do make plastic lenses that fit over the plate, and those screen things that make the plate only legible when viewed directly perpendicular to it, but those are illegal everywhere.
